description: We're a student team working on the challenge about identifying Earth locations that are analogous to potential Moon and Mars base locations. We're interested in science, research, data, space exploration and technology. We're looking for teammates interested in coding, data analysis, research, design, visualization or storytelling. You don't need to be an expert we're here to learn and build something together.
summary:
Analog Atlas is a web-based platform developed to explore locations on Earth that could serve as analogs for potential Moon and Mars landing sites and future base locations.

Our project brings together 11 curated analog profiles, allowing users to explore different terrestrial environments and understand how their characteristics may relate to conditions beyond Earth. It is designed to make the exploration of these locations more accessible by presenting relevant information in one place.

The project addresses the NASA Space Apps challenge by connecting Earth's diverse landscapes with the needs of future lunar and Martian exploration. Studying Earth-based analogs can help researchers understand environmental conditions, identify potential challenges, and make more informed decisions when planning future missions.

We believe this matters because space exploration doesn't begin only when we reach another world. It also begins here on Earth, by observing, researching, and learning from the environments we already know. Analog Atlas is our attempt to make that connection easier to explore.
details: Analog Atlas was developed as an interactive web-based exploration platform to help people discover places on Earth that can serve as analogs for the Moon and Mars. The idea is to look at our own planet to better understand the environments, terrain and challenges that may be relevant to future space exploration. The website currently features 11 curated analog profiles. Each profile offers a starting point for exploring a terrestrial location and understanding why it may be relevant to lunar or Martian research. Rather than presenting these locations as confirmed landing sites, our project encourages users to explore their similarities and research potential. One of the main benefits of Analog Atlas is that it brings different locations and their information together in one place. It can serve as an accessible starting point for students, space enthusiasts and anyone interested in planetary science. In the long term, we hope the project can encourage further research and help people appreciate how studying Earth can contribute to planning future missions. We developed the project using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON and Node.js, with GitHub for code management and Railway for deployment. Canva was used to prepare our project presentation. Our creative approach was to turn the idea of terrestrial analog research into an accessible exploration experience. We considered the relevance of each location, the clarity of the information, ease of navigation and the importance of not overstating scientific conclusions. Analog Atlas is currently a prototype, and we see it as a foundation that can be expanded with more verified data, research references and functionality. For us, the central idea is simple: before exploring another world, there is a lot we can learn by studying our own.
